concept_card.statement: Each particle does SHM in place; the wave pattern moves at a speed set by the medium, not the source.
concept_card.analogy: Stadium Mexican wave: fans only stand and sit, yet the wave runs round.
steps: Particles oscillate about their own mean positions
Pattern and energy pass from particle to particle
Medium sets speed: v = √(T/μ) on a string
Source sets f; amplitude leaves v unchanged

remediation_cards.wrong_idea: The wave carries the rope (or water, or air) along with it to the other end.
remediation_cards.why_it_feels_right: You can see something moving forward, and waves at the beach seem to push things to the shore.
remediation_cards.why_wrong: Each piece of the medium only moves up-down or back-forth about its own place. Only the pattern and energy move forward.
remediation_cards.correct_idea: The medium stays put and oscillates; the disturbance is what travels.
remediation_cards.sim_moment: Red-Dot Rope: the red dot bobs up and down as the wave runs past, never moving along.

remediation_cards.wrong_idea: If I shake the rope faster, the wave will run along it faster.
remediation_cards.why_it_feels_right: Moving your hand faster feels like more effort, so it seems the wave should be quicker too.
remediation_cards.why_wrong: On a string v = √(T/μ), set only by tension and mass per length. Shaking faster raises f, so λ = v/f shrinks instead.
remediation_cards.correct_idea: Higher frequency gives shorter waves moving at the same speed.
remediation_cards.sim_moment: Red-Dot Rope: raise the frequency slider and see the crests bunch closer while the front still reaches the end at the same time.

remediation_cards.wrong_idea: If I shake harder and make bigger waves, they will travel faster.
remediation_cards.why_it_feels_right: A bigger push usually makes things go faster, like throwing a ball harder.
remediation_cards.why_wrong: Amplitude does not appear in v = √(T/μ). A taller wave carries more energy, but on the same rope it moves at the same speed.
remediation_cards.correct_idea: Bigger amplitude means more energy, not more speed.
remediation_cards.sim_moment: Red-Dot Rope: raise the amplitude slider and see the taller pulse reach the end at the same moment as a small one.

contrast_probes.probe: If you shake a rope faster, where does a red dot painted on its middle end up after a minute?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It gets carried down to the far end along with the wave.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It stays near its spot and just jiggles faster.

contrast_probes.probe: What decides how soon a pulse on a rope reaches the far end?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: How fast the rope itself gets dragged forward.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: How big the pulse is; a bigger one gets there sooner.

contrast_probes.probe: On the same rope, one pulse is tall but slowly made and the other is small but quickly made. Which reaches the end first?
After a wave has fully passed a ribbon tied to the middle of a rope, where is the ribbon?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Further along the rope, closer to the far end.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Back at the same spot; it only went up and down.

contrast_probes.probe: Same rope, same tension: you double how many times per second you shake it. What happens to the wave speed?
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It stays the same; the waves just get shorter.

contrast_probes.probe: Same rope, same tension: you make the pulse twice as tall. Does it reach the far end sooner?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Yes, the bigger pulse gets there sooner.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: No, it arrives at the same time, just taller.

verify_flags: Amplitude-independence of v holds for small (linear) waves only
Sound speed 343 m/s at about 20 °C used in items; NCERT also quotes 331 m/s at 0 °C
W1 'beach waves push things to shore' in why_it_feels_right: real water waves do cause slight drift; kept as the student's intuition, not as physics
